title: Arjuna's fear for the family
hookLine: Arjuna fears a war will wipe out the ways a family keeps: kuladharma
carry: dharma lives in what a family keeps
tomorrow: how does chapter one end: with a battle, or a man sitting down?

lines: A RECIPE CARD IN THE GROUP CHAT.
cards: A photo lands in the family group chat: a recipe card in a great-grandmother's handwriting, the corners soft, a turmeric stain on one edge. Within minutes, three cousins want it. Nobody is fighting about the food.
They're fighting about what goes missing if the card does. Cut to a chariot between two armies. Arjuna has just told Krishna he doesn't want to win, and he hasn't stopped talking.
He's reached a new fear, and it isn't about the men who will die. It's about what dies after them.

teach.h: KULA + KSHAYA: IN A FAMILY'S RUIN.
teach.b: Here's his line: kulakshaye pranashyanti kuladharmah sanatanah. Find the seams. Kulakshaye is kula, family, plus kshaya, ruin: in the ruin of a family.
Kuladharmah: kula again, plus dharma, so a family's dharma, the duties and rites a family keeps. Sanatanah: long-standing. When a family is ruined, its long-standing ways perish.
Here's one to tell someone tonight. Some Hindus today call their whole tradition sanatana dharma. In this verse, sanatana isn't a name.

It describes the ways one family keeps. The verses after it carry the fear further: when dharma is lost, disorder overtakes the family, and the rites for the ancestors, the offerings of rice and water, go undone.
Now the teaching under the grammar. Dharma isn't only a law written in a book.

teach.h: THE LAMP, THE RITES, THE PRAYER.
teach.b: Hindus keep it at home: the lamp lit at dusk, the shraddha rites for the ancestors, the prayer a grandmother taught. That's kuladharma, and it's why Arjuna's fear is real. Readers hear him two ways.
Some hear real grief for everything a war erases beyond the dead. Some hear a frightened man reaching for any argument that might stop the fight.
Krishna will answer with another dharma, Arjuna's own duty. But the fear itself names something every Hindu home knows.

how: Many Hindu families keep household rites handed down through generations, such as a lamp lit at dusk and shraddha rites for the ancestors: the kind of family dharma Arjuna names in chapter one.

games.q: what does “reading the gita's first chapter” mean?
o: the Gita's later chapter on the ancestors
Krishna telling Arjuna that family ways don't matter
Arjuna fearing a war will erase the dharma a family keeps

games.q: the long words, split — tap the pairs.

s: in Gita 1.40, sanatana is the name of the Hindu religion
here it describes kuladharmah: the long-standing ways of a family.
Krishna is the one who makes this family argument
it's Arjuna's argument; Krishna answers him later.
kulakshaye splits into kula, family, and kshaya, ruin
a compound: in the ruin of a family.

games.q: your cousin says dharma is just a big word from old books. what does Gita 1.40 show her?
o: dharma also lives in a family's ways: the lamp, the rites, the prayers kept at home.
dharma only means the law of the universe; it has nothing to do with families.
dharma means whatever a family happens to like doing.
games.why: kuladharmah: a family's dharma. Arjuna's fear is that a war will end the rites and ways a household keeps.

practice: On any scrap of paper, write by hand one small way a family you love keeps: a dish, a greeting, a prayer, how a lamp gets lit. Underneath, write whose hands it came through. If you pray, say their names.
Then set the pen down and breathe with the page in front of you.

wordCard.voice: Kuladharmah sanatanah: a family's long-standing ways, the dharma Arjuna fears a war will erase. Reading the Gita's first chapter, one line at a time.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: kuladharma, family dharma, a compound of kula, family, and dharma.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma lives in what a family keeps. Arjuna feared losing it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.40–1.44 (when dharma is lost, adharma overcomes the family; the chain Arjuna fears, including rites for the ancestors)
